This explanation. The view is that you have two valuable human lives right here. It isn't like, well, we'll do what the mom wants because of bodily rights, or we'll do what the mom wants because the unborn is nothing or just a lump of tissue or something attacking the woman, like a disease or whatever. And these are all ways that people have used to justify abortion. No, we are acknowledging fully and completely that we have two fully valuable human beings in view here because in fact, we do. Well, the child's life is probably endangered too. Mom's carrying the baby. And if mom can't survive, the baby's not going to survive. And so the question here is not whether it is how do we do the most good and how do we save lives? As things are moving ahead with the idea that this is in fact a lethal circumstance for mom, what we stipulated, then baby's not going to survive either. And the goal here is not to take a life. The intention here is not to take a life. The goal and the intention is to save a life. And that is the life that can be saved. And that would be the mother's. In the circumstance of the baby, given the stipulation, that baby's life is going to be lost. And so the question here is, how do we save a life? And the answer is, we terminate the pregnancy to save the life of the mother. Now, there is a moral principle that's in play here. And it's called the law of double effect. And it's, it sounds fancy schmancy the way I'm talking about it. Oh, he's got a degree of philosophy. He can talk like that. But it's something we're all well aware of. Do you know, for example, that on D-Day, June 6th, 1944, that on the D-Day invasion of Europe to free Europe from the stranglehold that the Third Reich had on it and all of the atrocities that resulted from that, not just with Jews, but so many others. In order to free them, we had to attack. We had to land on the coast of France at Normandy. But before the landing, there was a bombardment. The big guns totally bombarded the beach. And it made it possible for there to be a landing that was successful. And in that bombing and subsequent bombing and the invasion on D-Day of Normandy and all of Europe, ultimately, something like 30,000 French citizens were killed. Now, did Eisenhower at all know that all of these citizens would die? Sure. Did they want them to die? No. We don't want to kill French citizens. We're trying to save French citizens. But how do you save French citizens and the rest of Europe? You've got to invade at Normandy, and invading at Normandy with the intention of freeing French citizens will kill French citizens, some, to free the rest. And there was no way to avoid that. And the principle of the, or I should say, the law of double effect comes into play in a circumstance like this because we acknowledge the full humanity of all those citizens and their full value as human beings. And we have an intention to free valuable human beings from the scourge of the Nazi occupation. But we understand that though we are acting in such a way as to save those lives, we realize there is a foreseen and unintended consequence. And that unintended consequence is that there are going to be citizens, French citizens, that will lose their life in the invasion. They'll get caught in the crossfire. It's called friendly fire. We know that happens. It cannot be avoided in war. But you live with that consequence. You live with that reality, and you are morally justified in doing the good thing that you intend, even though the bad thing that you don't intend is a consequence that you know will take place. Law of double effect. And so in the circumstances of when a mother's life is in danger, it's the same thing. If the pregnancy is terminated, it's to save a life. Otherwise, you're going to have two corpses instead of one. And even though the death of the child is foreseen, it is not intended. The thing that is intended is to save the mother's life. It was possible to save the child. They'd do that too. But as per stipulation, this is a circumstance where the child is not going to survive, and mom isn't going to survive either. So this is the deal. It's just not an abortion like that. It is an act to save a life of a woman, though there is an unintended consequence that the child will lose his or her life in the process. And in that case, it's more acceptable because of that kind of thing. And incidentally, this type of dilemma is encountered regularly in life, usually not when there's so much at stake, like a human life or two human lives in this case. But nevertheless, we are weighing options and alternatives and we're saying, okay, if we're going to do this, this will be the consequence. We don't like the consequence, but we're going to live with the consequence because the other thing is so much more morally weighty. And we don't even think most of the time about how this might apply to the abortion issue, but it is applicable in this set of circumstances. Okay. So when I said that, that seemed to be adequate for the first student.
